title: Static Libraries
summary: A **static library** (`.lib`) is a bundle of object files. Linking it into a program copies in the parts the program uses, so the result is one self-contained `.exe`. This lesson builds the course's `engine` library, shows how the linker pulls code out of it, and covers the settings that must match between a library and the program that uses it.
markdown:
## A bundle of object files When a project's **Configuration Type** is **Static library (.lib)**, its build stops after compiling: instead of linking the object files into an executable, the **librarian** (`lib.exe`) packs them into one `.lib` file with an index of the symbols each defines. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["math.cpp"] --> AO["math.obj"] B["tilemap.cpp"] --> BO["tilemap.obj"] C["random.cpp"] --> CO["random.obj"] AO --> L["lib.exe"] BO --> L CO --> L L --> LIB["engine.lib
(index + 3 object files)"] ``` When a program links against `engine.lib`, the linker looks up each unresolved symbol in the index and copies in **only the object files that define what is needed**. If the game never calls anything in `random.obj`, none of it ends up in the `.exe`. ## Building the engine library In the course solution from lesson 4.01, `engine` is already a static library project. Give it some real code: ```cpp // engine/vec2.h #pragma once struct Vec2 { float x{ 0 }; float y{ 0 }; }; Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b); Vec2 operator*(Vec2 v, float s); float length(Vec2 v); ``` ```cpp // engine/vec2.cpp #include "vec2.h" #include Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b) { return { a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y }; } Vec2 operator*(Vec2 v, float s) { return { v.x * s, v.y * s }; } float length(Vec2 v) { return std::sqrt(v.x * v.x + v.y * v.y); } ``` ```cpp // game/main.cpp #include #include "vec2.h" int main() { Vec2 position{ 1, 2 }; Vec2 velocity{ 3, 4 }; position = position + velocity * 0.5f; std::cout << position.x << ", " << position.y << " speed " << length(velocity) << '\n'; return 0; } ``` With the project reference and include directory from lesson 4.01 in place, building the solution builds `engine.lib` first, then compiles `main.cpp` and links it with `engine.lib`. The output prints `2.5, 4 speed 5`. Without a project reference (for example, a library someone else built), you tell the linker yourself: - **Linker → General → Additional Library Directories**: the folder containing the `.lib`; - **Linker → Input → Additional Dependencies**: the file name, `engine.lib`; - or, in code, `#pragma comment(lib, "engine.lib")`. ## Settings that must match Object files compiled with different settings may not work together, and the linker catches some (not all) of these mismatches: | Setting | Must match because | Mismatch error | |---|---|---| | Platform (x64 / x86) | 64-bit and 32-bit code cannot be mixed | LNK1112: module machine type conflicts | | Runtime library (`/MD`, `/MDd`, `/MT`, `/MTd`) | Each object file asks for a particular C runtime; they must agree | LNK2038: mismatch detected for 'RuntimeLibrary' | | Debug / Release (`_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL`) | Standard containers have different layouts in Debug and Release | LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' | | C++ standard, struct packing, other defines that change layout | A class laid out differently in two files is a silent ODR violation | Usually none: just strange crashes | The `LNK2038` checks exist because these mismatches used to cause baffling crashes: a `std::vector` passed from a Release library to Debug code has a different layout on each side. So **build every library in the same configuration as the program**. A project reference does this automatically; a pre-built library usually ships in both Debug and Release forms for this reason. The **runtime library** choice deserves a note. `/MD` links the C and C++ runtime as DLLs (the user needs the Visual C++ Redistributable installed); `/MT` copies the runtime into your executable. Either is fine for this course; just be consistent across every project in the solution. ## Static libraries versus DLLs | | Static library | DLL (next lesson) | |---|---|---| | When code is joined | At link time, copied into the `.exe` | At run time, loaded from a separate file | | Files to ship | Just the `.exe` | The `.exe` and every `.dll` | | Updating the library | Rebuild and relink the program | Replace the `.dll` | | Loading code chosen at run time (plugins) | Not possible | Possible | | Sharing between programs | Each program has its own copy | One file can be shared | The course uses a static library for the engine, which the game always needs, and a DLL for plugins, which the game chooses to load. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Linking a Debug library into a Release program > `LNK2038` warns you. Use project references, or link the matching build of the library. > [!warning] Expecting a static library to work without its headers > The `.lib` holds code; your program still needs the declarations from its headers to call it. > [!warning] Global objects in a static library that nothing references > The linker only pulls in object files that define something needed. A self-registering global in an otherwise unreferenced `.obj` is silently left out. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? How does the linker decide which parts of a static library go into the program? - It copies the whole library into every program + It takes each object file that defines a symbol still needed - It copies only the functions named in the project settings - It copies nothing; the library is loaded at run time > Unused object files are left out, which is why a program using one function from a large library stays small. It repeats until nothing more is needed, so unused object files are left out. ? Why must a library be built with the same runtime library and configuration as the program? + Mismatches disagree about the runtime and standard type layouts - Otherwise the linker cannot find the `.lib` file - Because the library's functions would run in a different process - Because Visual Studio only allows one configuration per solution > LNK2038 "mismatch detected" errors are the linker catching exactly this. ? When would you choose a DLL over a static library? - When you want the program to start faster - When the library is small and only used by one program - When you want every function inlined into the program + When code must be loaded or replaced at run time, as with plugins > A static library is copied into each program at link time; a DLL stays a separate file loaded when needed. ? What does a static library contain? - A finished program - Only header files + Object files and an index of their symbols > It is an archive of compiled code, ready to be linked. ? The game uses only `length` from `engine.lib`. What gets copied into `game.exe`? + The object file that defines `length`, and what it needs - The whole library - Nothing; it is loaded at run time > The linker pulls in object files on demand, by symbol. ? `LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL'`. What does it mean? - The library was built as 32-bit code + Debug-built and Release-built code are mixed - A function in the library is missing > Debug and Release standard containers have different layouts; mixing them is unsafe. ```
ideas:
- Add the `Vec2` files to your `engine` project and use them from `game`. Check the output is `2.5, 4  speed 5`.
- Change only `engine` to **Multi-threaded (/MT)** in **C/C++ → Code Generation → Runtime Library** and read the linker error. Change it back.
- Run `lib /list engine.lib` in the Developer PowerShell to see the object files inside.

cards.q: How does the linker decide which parts of a static library go into the program?
cards.a:
It takes each object file that defines a symbol still needed

Unused object files are left out, which is why a program using one function from a large library stays small. It repeats until nothing more is needed, so unused object files are left out.

cards.q: Why must a library be built with the same runtime library and configuration as the program?
cards.a:
Mismatches disagree about the runtime and standard type layouts

LNK2038 "mismatch detected" errors are the linker catching exactly this.

cards.q: When would you choose a DLL over a static library?
cards.a:
When code must be loaded or replaced at run time, as with plugins

A static library is copied into each program at link time; a DLL stays a separate file loaded when needed.

cards.q: What does a static library contain?
cards.a:
Object files and an index of their symbols

It is an archive of compiled code, ready to be linked.

cards.q: The game uses only `length` from `engine.lib`. What gets copied into `game.exe`?
cards.a:
The object file that defines `length`, and what it needs

The linker pulls in object files on demand, by symbol.

cards.q: `LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL'`. What does it mean?
cards.a:
Debug-built and Release-built code are mixed

Debug and Release standard containers have different layouts; mixing them is unsafe.
